title: Blogging with Quarto and Jupyter
text:
I enjoy the meta of bloggers writing about their blogging setup. So here’s mine.


Why Quarto
Quarto is a publishing system built on top of Pandoc. It renders Markdown, R Markdown, and Jupyter notebooks into websites, PDFs, or slide decks. For a data scientist, that means you can write a post that includes real code, real output, and real figures — all in one document, with no copy-pasting.
The previous generation of this was R Markdown, which worked well but was R-only. Quarto is language-agnostic: Python, R, Julia, and Observable all work.


Jupyter notebooks as posts
One thing I particularly like: you can use .ipynb files directly as posts. Write your analysis in a notebook, add a YAML header, and Quarto publishes it. No conversion step, no reformatting.
This matters because it keeps the source of truth in one place. The notebook is the post.


The setup
This site is built with:

Quarto for rendering
GitHub Actions for automated deployment on every push
GitHub Pages for hosting

The workflow is simple: write a post, push to main, and it goes live. The whole pipeline is visible in the repo.


What I’d change
The main friction so far is freezing: Quarto caches executed outputs so you don’t re-run expensive code on every build. That’s good in principle but occasionally produces stale outputs if you’re not careful. Something to watch.

title: What I care about
text:
What drives the work I choose to do? I’ve been a physicist, then became a data scientist, and along the way I’ve developed a fairly clear sense of what I want to spend my time on. Three ideas keep coming back, and they all happen to start with E.


Equity
Not equity in the financial sense — equity as in fairness and justice. I grew up in the Netherlands with a lot of advantages I didn’t earn: citizenship, education, stable family. That background took a while to fully appreciate. The more I learned about how colonialism, racism, and structural inequality shape life outcomes, the harder it became to work on things that don’t engage with that somehow.
Climate justice is a good example of where this gets concrete: the people most affected by environmental damage are rarely those most responsible for it.


Ecology
Things are connected. That’s the core of it. Ecology as a value means taking systems thinking seriously — not just in the biological sense, but in how economies, communities, and institutions interact. Diversity, circular systems, long feedback loops: these matter.
It also just means I’d rather work outdoors than not, and I find organisms more interesting than most software.


Evidence
I like data. I think clearly gathered and honestly presented evidence is one of the better tools we have for making decisions and having arguments. Which is not to say data is neutral — it isn’t — but the discipline of being honest about uncertainty and transparent about methods is worth something.
This is probably why I ended up as a data scientist.


In practice
These three things together mean I look for work that uses careful analysis to address real inequity or ecological problems. That’s the short version of why I do what I do.

title: About
text:
I’m Sebas Eliëns, an independent data scientist based in the Netherlands. My background is in physics, and I now work on data and analysis projects — mostly in areas related to sustainability and social issues.
This site is where I share work, notes, and the occasional longer piece. If you have a project that could use a data scientist, feel free to get in touch.
